newsitem.title: USA: Ahmanson sees more revenues, cost savings.
newsitem.headline: Ahmanson sees more revenues, cost savings.

text.p: H.F. Ahmanson and Co, which enhanced its bid for Great Western Financial Corp Monday, also said it revised its cost savings, revenue and earnings projections regarding the merger.

Ahmanson said it raised Ahmanson's standalone earnings estimates due to an increase in consensus estimates and Great Western's standalone estimates to reflect data presented by rival suitor Washington Mutual Savings Bank, which used higher earnings estimates.
Ahmanson also said cost savings from the merger would be up by at least $50 million to $454 million.
Ahmnanson, which had not built any revenue enhancements into its original proposal, said it now assumed at least $50 million in revenue enhancements due to the merger.

"Our assumptions continue to be conservative and believable," chief finanical officer Kevin Twomey said on a conference call. "Our belief our original merger benefit numbers were understated by at least $100 million in general and administrative (cost) and revenues is predicated on information released by Washington Mutual and Great Western subsequent to our proposal and not based on a change in our underlying assumptions," said Twomey.

"While we're committed to pursuing this offer, we fully expect this revised proposal will require Great Western's board to netogiate with us under the stardard set forth in the Washington Mutual proposal," Twomey said.
The enhanced proposal establishes a floating exchange ratio of 1.10 to 1.20 shares of Ahmanson for each Great Western share, up from the original exchange ratio of 1.05.

Ahmanson Monday revised its projections to say the merger would produce nine percent to 15 percent accretion to cash earnings per share in 1998 and 22 percent to 29 percent accretion to cash earnings in 1999.
Under the original bid, the projected cash earnings per share accretion of five percent in 1997, 15 percent in 1998 and 26 percent in 1999, a spokesman said.

Ahmanson said the merger would dilute earnings on a reported basis in 1998 by seven percent to 11 percent and would be accretive to reported earnings per share in 1999 by three percent to seven percent.
"The latest proposal was designed to build certainty back into the marketplace about Ahmanson's ability to succeed," said Ahmanson's chief executive officer Charles Rinehart.
